articles.title: India’s 5th-gen stealth AMCA aircraft: Bids of 3 consortiums submitted, evaluation under way
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: In a big step towards developing India’s fifth-generation stealth fighter aircraft, three Indian contenders have submitted bids to a high-level
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a big step towards developing India’s fifth-generation stealth fighter aircraft, three Indian contenders have submitted bids to a high-level review committee constituted by the defence ministry for prototype development for the Rs 15,000-crore Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft programme with their evaluation process now on.Industry sources confirmed to TOI that the three contenders — L&T-led consortium of BEL and Dynamatic, Tata Advanced Systems Ltd (TASL), and Bharat Forge-led consortium of BEML Ltd and Data Patterns — submitted their individual bids on Oct 30, the deadline for submission. Of the three, only TASL is the solitary bidder.“The bids were opened on Nov 1 to select a development-cum-production partner (DCPP) for developing five AMCA prototypes (designed by DRDO laboratory Aeronautical Development Agency),” the sources told TOI. The Bengaluru-based ADA, which conceived the project, will oversee the manufacturing of five twin-engine AMCA prototypes.The AMCA is likely to be powered by twin F414 engines if the proposed deal between defence PSU Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd and US-based GE for their joint production in India materialises. ADA requires 15 F414 engines for five flying prototypes for the AMCA project.The five prototypes are expected to undertake 1,800 test sorties in a period of seven years to validate the fighter’s flight-control systems, stealth characteristics, sensors, radar, weapons integration and propulsion performance.AMCA, once ready, will help the Indian Air Force acquire the fifth-generation fighter jet at a time. However, the first batch of the AMCA is expected to be ready around 2034 or 2035. AMCA is also meant to plug the shortfall in the IAF fighter squadrons, which have already come down to an alarming 29 against a sanctioned strength of 42.5. The deadline was earlier extended from Aug 27 to Oct 30 after bidders sought more time to complete formalities for the complex stealth aircraft programme. The aircraft’s stealth features include internal weapons bays, supercruise capability, advanced AI-driven avionics and next-generation sensor fusion.China is already operating two primary fifth-generation stealth fighter jets, Chengdu J-20 and the Shenyang J-35, and Pakistan is also planning to buy 40 Chinese J-35 stealth aircraft.

articles.title: Steering failure preceded New Orleans cruise ship collision, says NTSB
articles.summary: Preliminary findings by National Transportation Safety Board investigators suggest the tanker suffered a "steering casualty" before colliding with the cruise ship on Friday.
articles.body:
The tanker that struck a cruise ship docked in New Orleans on Friday had a steering failure, officials said, citing preliminary findings into the collision.

It remains unclear what caused the "steering casualty" on the Atlantic Asphalt cargo vessel, the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said in a media briefing on Sunday.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken American Heritage riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one was unaccounted for.

The NTSB said there are many different things that could be classified as a steering casualty, and they are "looking at all of them".

New Orleans port files $1m lawsuit over 'miracle on the Mississippi' tanker collision

The tanker was upbound on the Mississippi River as it moved toward the east bank of the river just before the collision, said the NTSB, based on findings from the vessel's voyage data recorder.

Minutes before the crash, investigators said audio consistent with the ship's warning system was broadcast, along with commands to deploy the vessel's anchors and emergency ship handling orders.

"We are aware that there was an issue with the steering on board and causing the rudder to remain at a starboard position, causing the heading of the vessel to veer towards the east bank," investigator-in-charge Bart Barnum said during the news conference.

The exact issue with the steering has yet to be determined, he added.

A preliminary report from the NTSB is expected in 30 days.

Calls about the collision began around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday, when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans chief Melanie Montroll said after the incident.

There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.

Passengers began getting off the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping onto its side.

Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.

The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

articles.title: An investor bought a Palm Beach site for $9 million in 2023 and built a seven-bedroom mansion; the new home is now under contract for $32 million amid a foreclosure suit
articles.summary: A newly completed mansion at 301 Plantation Road in Palm Beach is on the market with an asking price of $32 million.
articles.body: A newly completed mansion at 301 Plantation Road in Palm Beach is on the market with an asking price of $32 million. It is the most expensive of 21 luxury deals signed across Palm Beach County between Nov. 2 and Nov. 8, and it is at the centre of a foreclosure case that began in October, The Real Deal reported. The seller is an LLC managed by investment banker Roberto de Guardiola. The entity paid $9 million for the property in 2023, according to public records.This year, it fell behind on a $22 million mortgage, and the lender responded by filing a foreclosure suit in October. The house itself was completed this year. Margit Brandt of Premier Estate Properties holds the listing and is often ranked among the top two brokers in Palm Beach by sales volume.A Palm Beach estate completed this yearThe brand-new estate is on the North End of Palm Beach Island. The listing on Redfin says it was completed in spring 2026. It spans more than 9,000 square feet and has seven bedrooms, eight full bathrooms and three half-bathrooms. The ceilings measure 11.5 feet, giving the formal rooms plenty of height and making the home ideal for entertaining. The kitchen is equipped with Gaggenau and Sub-Zero appliances.The primary suite is particularly luxurious and includes two marble bathrooms, custom closets, a fireplace and private terraces. Outdoors, a covered loggia with its own fireplace overlooks a 54-foot double infinity-edge pool, with a spa and cabana nearby. Vesta Home staged the interiors, and every piece is available for purchase. The house's modern conveniences include an elevator, a two-car air-conditioned garage with separate service parking, a generator, automated shades, impact windows and a full security system.A busy week at the top of the marketThe high-end market remained active this week, according to Douglas Elliman's Eklund Gomes team, which tracks every residential listing in the county priced above $3 million. Buyers signed 21 contracts, with a combined asking volume of $206.5 million. The week before, 17 contracts carried $202.7 million.Sixteen of the new contracts were for single-family homes. Those houses totalled $174.8 million in asking volume, or about $10.9 million on average. They averaged $1,884 per square foot and had spent an average of 244 days on the market before going under contract, a long wait compared with the rest of the group.The other five contracts were for condominiums. Their asking volume came to $31.8 million, an average of $6.4 million each, or $2,421 per square foot. Those units had spent an average of 32 days on the market. Condominiums were therefore selling considerably faster than houses this week, and the gap in days on the market is one of the clearest patterns in the figures.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: US govt seeks 24-year jail, Nikhil Gupta pleads for 12
articles.summary: US State Department is learnt to have asked for 24 years in jail for Nikhil Gupta, the Indian national facing trial for an alleged assassination attempt
articles.body: US State Department is learnt to have asked for 24 years in jail for Nikhil Gupta, the Indian national facing trial for an alleged assassination attempt on designated terrorist and chief of Sikhs For Justice group Gurpatwant Singh Pannun.Gupta's counsel have requested a reduced sentence of 12 years while submitting a remorse letter to the judge ahead of sentencing Nov 20. They have requested the judge to consider the probation department's recommendation of a similar-duration jail term besides Gupta pleading guilty and not wasting the court's time. Prosecutors have, however, asked to consider his act of planning a murder on foreign soil as brazen and asked for the maximum sentence.If he gets more than 12 months, Gupta may be eligible for term reduction of up to 15%Nikhil Gupta has claimed to be a victim of deception and claimed that he was promised by an individual to settle cases in exchange for plotting the killing.In Feb, Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty to charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit it, and money laundering conspiracy which carry a statutory jail term of around 40 years. With this, he may be looking at a reduced sentence through an "acceptance of responsibility" credit.Gupta (54), sources said, may receive a two- to three-level reduction, the standard reward for saving the court the time and expense of a trial. "But if US prosecutors prevail, a 20-year sentence seems likely. Gupta may have to serve around 80% of the awarded jail time with all parameters like good behaviour etc in place," said a source.Under the United States law, if he receives a sentence longer than 12 months, he would be eligible for up to a 15% reduction (roughly two months a year) for good behaviour while incarcerated. articles.title: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies age 80
articles.summary: Known as the 'Boss of Bosses', he was the head of all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel in the 1980s before his arrest broke up his drug organisation.
articles.body:
Notorious Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo has died in hospital aged 80.

Félix Gallardo was widely considered one of the biggest drug smugglers in history and is credited with building an alliance between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.

Known as The Godfather or the 'Boss of Bosses', Félix Gallardo was the head of the all-powerful Guadalajara Cartel, which reigned over Mexican drug trafficking at the height of the cocaine boom of the 1980s.

At the time, it created a new modus operandi in the illegal drug trade which endures to this day. He had been in state custody since 1989.

The name Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's.

He led the organisation which revolutionised drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly Escobar's Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.

At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the US came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organisation played a major role in smuggling it in.

At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo exerted huge influence over Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships.

In 1985, the net started to tighten around the leaders of the cartel following the torture and murder of a DEA agent, Enrique 'Kiki' Camarena.

Camarena had angered them after he had discovered and then destroyed a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua, which belonged to the criminal group.

His murder sparked one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America.

In 1989, Félix Gallardo was captured and sentenced to decades in prison. In ill health, he was granted house arrest in 2022 but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer. He died in hospital in his native Guadalajara.

In the 1980s, Joaquin 'El Chapo' Guzmán was introduced to Félix Gallardo, who put him in charge of handling logistics for his drug organisation.

From the subsequent break-up of Félix Gallardo's organisation after his arrest, the Sinaloa Cartel emerged, led by Guzmán, now another man synonymous with large-scale drug trafficking.

In 2019, Guzmán was sentenced to life in prison for charges including drug trafficking and money laundering following one of the most high-profile trials in recent US history.

Félix Gallardo's life has been portrayed in a number of television programmes including the Netflix series Narcos: Mexico. The show depicted his rise to power as well as his relationship with Guzmán.

articles.title: Teste de DNA para pets vira negócio e fatura R$ 300 mil por mês | G1
articles.standfirst: Após descobrir o potencial da genética, fundador investiu R$ 4 milhões em negócio que ajuda a prever doenças em cães e gatos.
articles.summary: Empresa usa genética para identificar predisposição a doenças em cães e gatos e ajudar veterinários na prevenção e no tratamento.
articles.body:
A história da Pet Genoma começou a partir da paixão de um empreendedor por animais e da vontade de transformar a genética em uma ferramenta de prevenção para cães e gatos.

A empresa realiza testes genéticos capazes de identificar centenas de predisposições a doenças, ajudando tutores e veterinários a tomar decisões mais assertivas sobre a saúde dos pets. O exame é feito por meio da coleta de saliva do animal e pode custar até R$ 790.

A ideia surgiu quando o fundador, Eduardo Lemes, passou a estudar genética e percebeu o potencial da tecnologia para o mercado pet.

A motivação ganhou ainda mais força após a lembrança de um cachorro da família que morreu em decorrência de uma cardiomiopatia dilatada, doença que, segundo ele, poderia ter sido identificada mais cedo com o auxílio de um teste genético.

“Quando eu entendi que aquilo era uma oportunidade de negócio, me vieram algumas lembranças importantes. Uma delas era do Grizzly, meu cachorro boxer, que morreu de uma doença chamada cardiomiopatia dilatada. Talvez isso pudesse ter sido evitado se a gente tivesse feito, por exemplo, um teste genético nele", conta o empreendedor Eduardo Lemes.

Hoje, a empresa opera um laboratório instalado em parceria com uma universidade e utiliza mais de 120 mil marcadores genéticos para analisar cada amostra.

Com um investimento inicial de cerca de R$ 4 milhões , o negócio construiu uma base de dados com milhares de animais e mantém parceria com 118 clínicas veterinárias em todo o país.

Empreendedor cria empresa de testes genéticos para pets e fatura R$ 300 mil por mês — Foto: Reprodução/PEGN

Os resultados ajudam a identificar riscos para doenças cardíacas, renais, oncológicas e outras condições que podem ser monitoradas e tratadas precocemente.

“São doenças que talvez não possamos evitar, mas podemos manejar o animal de tal modo que a gente pegue a doença muito no começo". explica o empreendedor.

Entre os clientes estão tutores como Vanessa Morais, que utilizou os testes em seus cães, Mila e Zion. A partir dos resultados, foi possível compartilhar informações com a veterinária responsável e desenvolver um acompanhamento personalizado para cada animal.

A ferramenta também vem sendo incorporada por clínicas veterinárias como suporte para diagnósticos, prognósticos e definição de estratégias de tratamento.

Com capacidade para processar um volume muito maior do que o atual, a empresa registra faturamento mensal de cerca de R$ 300 mil e aposta no crescimento da medicina veterinária preventiva.

“É uma empresa de genética e tecnologia para fazer nossos pets viverem mais e melhor", afirma o empreendedor. A expectativa do fundador é ampliar o uso da genética no setor e contribuir para que cães e gatos tenham uma vida mais longa e saudável.

“A gente tem vontade de olhar para trás e dizer que remodelou esse mercado para melhor. O dinheiro é bem-vindo, mas ele é consequência disso", completa Eduardo Lemes.

articles.title: Quem eram o casal e as duas crianças que morreram em acidente entre Kombi e caminhão a caminho de seminário no Paraná | G1
articles.standfirst: Vítimas eram pai, mãe e filho, além do filho de outro casal que estava no veículo. Famílias eram amigas e viajavam juntas para visitar seminário em Palmas quando a Kombi deslizou na pista e bateu em um caminhão.
articles.summary: Vítimas eram pai, mãe e filho, além do filho de outro casal que estava no veículo. Famílias eram amigas e viajavam juntas para visitar seminário em Palmas.
articles.body:
Jacir José Alves, Janice Gesser Alves, João Paulo Gesser Alves e Gabriel Luiz Schropfer — Foto: Cedidas pelas famílias

O casal e as duas crianças que morreram neste sábado (14) depois que a Kombi em que eles estavam bateu em um caminhão na PR-280 eram pai, mãe e filho, além do filho de outro casal que estava no veículo. Eles foram identificados como:

Jacir José Alves , de 47 anos (marido de Janice e pai de João Paulo);

Janice Gesser Alves , de 44 anos (esposa de Jacir e mãe de João Paulo);

João Paulo Gesser Alves , de 11 anos (filho de Janice e Jacir);

Gabriel Luiz Schropfer, de 9 anos (filho do casal sobrevivente).

Todos eram de Dois Vizinhos e viajavam juntos para visitar os filhos/irmãos mais velhos em um seminário de Palmas , cidade a cerca de 170 km de distância.

O acidente aconteceu em Mariópolis , no sudoeste do estado. O casal que sobreviveu foi socorrido com ferimentos, assim como o caminhoneiro. Relembre detalhes mais abaixo.

Janice era cadastrada como agricultora no Programa Nacional de Fortalecimento da Agricultura Familiar (Pronaf) e dona da loja de roupas de criança Kow Kids, de confecção própria.

O marido dela era apicultor, produtor do "Mel Alves", e também trabalhava como vendedor em uma loja de materiais de construção.

O casal que sobreviveu está se recuperando no hospital e não corre risco de morte, segundo familiares. A mulher fraturou uma costela e teve ferimentos nas pernas, e o homem fraturou diversas costelas e perfurou o intestino.

Kombi tinha seis ocupantes no momento da batida — Foto: Bruno Fernandes

Kombi rodou na pista molhada antes de bater no caminhão

A Kombi saiu da cidade de Dois Vizinhos e o acidente aconteceu cerca de um quilômetro depois do trevo de Mariópolis, sentido a Clevelândia .

As equipes de socorro afirmam que chovia no momento do acidente.

De acordo com o Corpo de Bombeiros, por volta das 15h30, a kombi deslizou na pista molhada e atingiu o guard-rail. Em seguida, o veículo bateu contra o caminhão, que vinha no sentido contrário.

Com a batida, o caminhão saiu da pista e a Kombi foi partida ao meio. Partes do veículo foram arrastadas por mais de 100 metros.

Os feridos foram encaminhados para unidades de saúde de Pato Branco .

Uma equipe de perícia esteve no local para determinar as causas do acidente.

Caminhão saiu da pista após a batida na PR-280. — Foto: Bruno Fernandes

A Prefeitura Municipal de Dois Vizinhos decretou luto oficial de três dias pelo falecimento dos quatro moradores. Em respeito à memória das vítimas e às famílias enlutadas, a abertura do Natal Iluminado, prevista para este domingo (15), foi adiada. A nova data será divulgada posteriormente.

Nas redes sociais, a prefeitura também expressou condolências aos familiares e amigos das vítimas e manifestou solidariedade a toda a comunidade duovizinhense.

"Rogamos a Deus que conceda serenidade e amparo a todos que enfrentam este momento de dor. Que as histórias de vida de quem partiu permaneçam vivas na memória de todos. Aos dois moradores hospitalizados, dedicamos uma palavra especial de carinho e solidariedade. Desejamos que encontrem conforto e força nos próximos dias e tenham uma plena recuperação", escreveu a prefeitura.

O Seminário São João Maria Vianney lamentou as mortes dos familiares dos seminaristas nas redes sociais.

"Neste momento de dor, pedimos a toda a comunidade que se una a nós em oração pelo descanso eterno de Janice, Jacir, João Paulo e Gabriel. Rezemos também pelos nossos seminaristas Júlio e Guilherme, por seus familiares e amigos. Que Deus lhes conceda consolo e força, e que Nossa Senhora os ampare neste tempo de luto. Dai-lhes, Senhor, o repouso eterno, e brilhe para eles a vossa luz. Descansem em paz. Amém".

articles.title: Eleição no Haiti: Viúva de Jovenel Moise registra candidatura | G1
articles.standfirst: Primeiro turno está previsto para julho do próximo ano, em meio à violência de gangues e à instabilidade política no país.
articles.summary: A eleição no Haiti terá Martine Moise como candidata à presidência; viúva de líder assassinado tenta pacificar o país em meio à crise e violência de gangues.
articles.body:
Martine Moïse é viúva de Jovenel Moïse, ex-presidente do Haiti — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Martine Moise, viúva do último presidente do Haiti, cujo assassinato em 2021 marcou uma importante virada para o país, registrou sua candidatura à primeira eleição presidencial haitiana em uma década, segundo mostrou o site do conselho eleitoral neste domingo (15).

O Haiti realizou sua última eleição presidencial em 2016. Desde então, sucessivos líderes, em meio à expansão da influência de gangues poderosas e fortemente armadas, adiaram repetidamente a votação, alegando falta de segurança.

O primeiro turno está marcado para julho do próximo ano.

"O Haiti voltará a se erguer por conta própria, porque a política precisa ser feita de maneira diferente", disse Moise na semana passada no X. Ela não comentou publicamente o registro da candidatura.

Moise é uma das três mulheres entre os 33 candidatos registrados. A lista inclui os ex-presidentes Michel Martelly e Jocelerme Privert, o ex-primeiro-ministro Claude Joseph e a ex-ministra das Relações Exteriores Dominique Dupuy.

Vários candidatos, entre eles Martelly e Privert, foram alvo de sanções internacionais por acusações de apoio a gangues armadas. Ambos negam irregularidades.

Moise é uma testemunha importante no processo que tramita em Miami contra dezenas de suspeitos de envolvimento no assassinato de Jovenel Moise , que governou o Haiti de 2017 até sua morte, em julho de 2021.

Ele foi morto a tiros em seu quarto por mercenários colombianos que se passaram por agentes da agência antidrogas dos Estados Unidos, a DEA. Martine Moise foi gravemente ferida a tiros e levada de avião para um hospital na Flórida.

Jovenel Moise durante uma entrevista em agosto de 2019 — Foto: Dieu Nalio Chery/Reuters

Após a morte do presidente, uma série de governos de transição assumiu o comando do país, enquanto gangues armadas, que se acredita amplamente serem apoiadas por políticos corruptos, tomaram o controle de grande parte da capital, Porto Príncipe, e de regiões próximas.

Desde 2022, cerca de 1,5 milhão de pessoas foram deslocadas e mais de 22 mil foram mortas, muitas pelas forças de segurança. Diversas forças internacionais foram enviadas ao Haiti para ajudar a polícia no combate às gangues. Mais recentemente, soldados de El Salvador foram mobilizados para o país.

Alguns políticos colocaram em dúvida a capacidade do atual governo de realizar uma eleição confiável.

O Fanmi Lavalas, partido historicamente influente liderado pelo ex-presidente Jean-Bertrand Aristide, deposto em um golpe em 2004, afirmou na sexta-feira que não lançará candidato enquanto as condições permanecerem tão incertas.

articles.summary: Caso ocorreu no sábado após pouso de aeronave vinda de Guarulhos. Piloto precisou acionar a torre de comando para relatar que família havia desembarcado sem o filho em Porto Alegre.
articles.body:
Uma criança de 7 anos que foi deixada em um avião no Aeroporto Internacional Salgado Filho, em Porto Alegre , ficou cerca de 15 minutos sob os cuidados da tripulação antes de ser entregue à mãe.

O caso ocorreu na tarde de sábado (14), após o desembarque de um voo vindo de São Paulo.

A situação foi revelada após o piloto da aeronave contatar a torre de controle para relatar o fato. No áudio, o comandante pede auxílio de um funcionário em solo.

'Tem uma situação meio inusitada aqui. Uma família desembarcou e esqueceu o filho a bordo aqui', comunicou o piloto.

A identidade dos familiares não foi divulgada.

A Latam Airlines Brasil, responsável pelo voo LA3420, que partiu de Guarulhos, confirmou a ocorrência. Em nota, a empresa declarou que a criança foi acompanhada por funcionários da companhia e devolvida em segurança à mãe após a confirmação do vínculo familiar.

"A LATAM Airlines Brasil esclarece que uma criança permaneceu a bordo do voo LA3420 (São Paulo/Guarulhos–Porto Alegre) deste sábado (14/11), após o desembarque de seus familiares. A criança foi acompanhada pela equipe da companhia e entregue em segurança à mãe, cerca de 15 minutos depois, após a confirmação do vínculo familiar."

Aeroporto Salgado Filho, em Porto Alegre, em abril de 2024 — Foto: Aryel Martins/ RBS TV

articles.standfirst: Fogo começou em prédio que abrigava empresa de aluguel de veículos e se espalhou para imóveis vizinhos.
articles.summary: Fogo começou em prédio que abrigava empresa de aluguel de veículos e se espalhou para imóveis vizinhos.
articles.body:
Um incêndio em um prédio comercial deixou 11 mortos e 16 feridos na ilha de Phuket, um dos principais destinos turísticos da Tailândia, na madrugada desta segunda-feira (16), segundo a polícia.

O fogo começou por volta das 3h17, no horário local, em um imóvel onde funcionava uma empresa de aluguel de veículos. As chamas se espalharam posteriormente para vários prédios próximos.

Segundo as autoridades tailandesas, os bombeiros levaram cerca de duas horas para controlar o incêndio.

Entre os 16 feridos, 15 são cidadãos da Tailândia e um é de Mianmar. De acordo com a polícia, nenhum turista está entre os mortos ou feridos.

O prédio atingido fica em uma área urbana próxima à praia de Patong, uma das mais conhecidas de Phuket, na costa oeste da ilha.

A causa do incêndio ainda não foi determinada e está sendo investigada pelas autoridades.

O caso ocorre quatro meses depois de outro incêndio de grandes proporções na Tailândia. Em julho, um incêndio em um bar de Bangkok deixou pelo menos 27 mortos .

articles.title: Concurso da Câmara dos Deputados encerra inscrições nesta semana; salários chegam a R$ 32 mil | G1
articles.standfirst: Com 66 vagas imediatas e 118 para cadastro de reserva, seleção terá provas em janeiro de 2027 e lotação dos aprovados em Brasília.
articles.summary: Com 66 vagas imediatas e 118 para cadastro de reserva, seleção terá provas em janeiro de 2027 e lotação dos aprovados em Brasília.
articles.body:
Câmara dos Deputados — Foto: Divulgação / Câmara dos Deputados

As inscrições para o novo concurso da Câmara dos Deputados terminam na próxima terça-feira (17).

A seleção reúne 184 oportunidades entre vagas imediatas e cadastro de reserva para profissionais de diferentes áreas, da comunicação às engenharias, além de cargos que aceitam diploma em qualquer graduação.

Os interessados devem se inscrever pelo site do Centro Brasileiro de Pesquisa em Avaliação e Seleção e de Promoção de Eventos (Cebraspe). O salário inicial é de R$ 32.070,88 para todas as especialidades da carreira de analista legislativo.

Entre as áreas contempladas estão Jornalismo, Relações Públicas, Arquivologia, Biblioteconomia, Museologia e diferentes especialidades de Engenharia.

O edital também prevê vagas para Registro e Redação, área que concentra a maior oferta de oportunidades e aceita diploma de curso superior em qualquer área reconhecida pelo Ministério da Educação (MEC).

O g1 preparou um guia com os principais pontos do concurso. Abaixo, entenda:

Embora todas as vagas pertençam à carreira de analista legislativo, o concurso não é destinado a um único perfil profissional.

Um dos destaques do edital é que a especialidade com maior número de vagas não exige formação superior específica.

A área de Registro e Redação oferece 25 vagas imediatas e outras 25 para cadastro de reserva. Para concorrer, basta possuir diploma de curso superior reconhecido pelo Ministério da Educação (MEC), independentemente da área de formação.

Já as demais oportunidades são destinadas a candidatos com graduações específicas.

O novo concurso da Câmara dos Deputados — Foto: g1

Independentemente da especialidade escolhida, todos os aprovados ingressarão na carreira com remuneração inicial de R$ 32.070,88 .

Os servidores serão lotados em Brasília, onde está localizada a sede da Câmara dos Deputados.

Além do salário, os ocupantes do cargo terão acesso aos benefícios oferecidos pela Casa e às garantias previstas para os servidores efetivos da administração pública federal.

Além da formação exigida para cada especialidade, os candidatos deverão atender aos requisitos legais para ingresso no serviço público federal.

ter nacionalidade brasileira ou portuguesa, nos casos previstos em lei;

estar em dia com as obrigações eleitorais;

estar quite com as obrigações militares, quando aplicável;

possuir aptidão física e mental para o exercício do cargo;

apresentar a documentação exigida para a posse;

possuir a graduação exigida para a especialidade escolhida.

Algumas áreas também exigem registro profissional no respectivo conselho de classe.

Embora todos os aprovados ingressem na carreira de analista legislativo, as atividades desempenhadas variam de acordo com a especialidade escolhida.

Os profissionais da área de Divulgação Institucional atuam na criação de campanhas, ações educativas e projetos de comunicação voltados à população.

Os jornalistas são responsáveis pela cobertura das atividades parlamentares, produção de reportagens, notícias, entrevistas e conteúdos para os diversos veículos de comunicação da Câmara.

Já os relações-públicas trabalham na organização de eventos, cerimônias, ações de relacionamento institucional e iniciativas voltadas ao fortalecimento da imagem da Casa.

Na área de gestão da informação , os arquivistas organizam e preservam documentos produzidos ao longo de décadas de atividade legislativa.

Os bibliotecários administram acervos e auxiliam em pesquisas técnicas utilizadas por parlamentares e servidores. Os museólogos, por sua vez, cuidam da preservação da memória institucional e dos bens históricos relacionados ao Poder Legislativo.

As especialidades de engenharia têm atribuições ligadas à manutenção e modernização da infraestrutura da Câmara. Os profissionais participam da elaboração de projetos, fiscalização de obras, emissão de pareceres técnicos e acompanhamento de contratos.

Já os servidores de Registro e Redação exercem uma das funções mais diretamente ligadas ao processo legislativo. Eles são responsáveis pelo registro oficial de debates, pronunciamentos e sessões parlamentares, além da elaboração, revisão e organização de documentos produzidos pela Casa.

As provas estão marcadas para 17 de janeiro de 2027 .

A aplicação ocorrerá nas 26 capitais brasileiras e no Distrito Federal. Dessa forma, os candidatos poderão realizar os exames em seus próprios estados, sem a necessidade de viajar para Brasília.

➡️ As avaliações serão aplicadas em dois turnos. Os horários definitivos serão divulgados posteriormente pelo Cebraspe.

A seleção será composta por prova objetiva e prova discursiva, ambas aplicadas no mesmo dia.

A prova objetiva terá 180 itens no formato "certo" ou "errado", distribuídos entre conhecimentos gerais e conhecimentos específicos.

Já a prova discursiva será voltada para conteúdos relacionados à especialidade escolhida pelo candidato.

Quando os aprovados poderão ser convocados?

A Câmara dos Deputados poderá iniciar as nomeações após a homologação do resultado final do concurso. Segundo o cronograma oficial, a divulgação do resultado final está prevista para 30 de abril de 2027.

A partir dessa data, as nomeações poderão ocorrer de acordo com as necessidades da administração e a disponibilidade de vagas.

Além dos candidatos classificados dentro das vagas imediatas, aprovados no cadastro de reserva também poderão ser convocados durante o período de validade do concurso, que será de dois anos - contados a partir da homologação do resultado final.

Esse prazo poderá ser prorrogado uma única vez, por igual período. Isso significa que a Câmara dos Deputados poderá convocar aprovados por até quatro anos, conforme suas necessidades administrativas.

O concurso prevê 118 oportunidades para cadastro de reserva, mecanismo utilizado para formar uma lista de candidatos aptos a serem convocados futuramente. Ou seja, quem for aprovado para o cadastro de reserva não tem direito à nomeação imediata.

Esses candidatos ficam em uma espécie de lista de espera e podem ser chamados caso surjam novas vagas, ocorram aposentadorias, exonerações ou haja necessidade de reforçar o quadro de servidores durante o período de validade do concurso.

A convocação segue a ordem de classificação e pode ocorrer a qualquer momento enquanto o concurso estiver válido.

15 de outubro a 17 de novembro de 2026: período de inscrições;

19 de novembro de 2026: prazo final para pagamento da taxa;

22 de dezembro de 2026: consulta aos locais de prova;

17 de janeiro de 2027: aplicação das provas objetiva e discursiva;

19 a 22 de janeiro de 2027: divulgação dos gabaritos preliminares;

18 de fevereiro de 2027: resultado das provas objetivas;

9 de abril de 2027: resultado provisório das provas discursivas;

30 de abril de 2027: resultado final do concurso.

articles.title: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a post-Putin future
articles.summary: Some Russian tycoons are pining after a return to a 1990s system of oligarchy, when businessmen enjoyed power
articles.body:
Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall.

More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask.

Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war.

"I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs."

In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word.

That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges.

And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves.

But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root.

The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, says he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country.

The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule". They had money, which back then meant power.

This era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "new Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent.

But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger.

Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, says the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there.

"I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin showed up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC.

Since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine). Their collective wealth has reached a new high of nearly $700bn (£525bn).

But even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless.

Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence.

"They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov says. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round."

And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion.

"They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," says Browder, the avowed Putin critic.

And so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons.

There's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health."

If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum.

In that scenario, Russia-watchers I have spoken with envisage a few potential scenarios.

Some in the West, and no doubt within Russia, hope that democracy might flourish in a post-Putin Russia, with government led by the people, rather than by a new cadre of oligarchs or a single autocrat. But this seems like the least likely path, analysts say. Key democratic institutions have been eroded or destroyed over Putin's rule. "Russia is so used to violence, it has grown unaccustomed to standard democratic procedures," says Alexandra Prokopenko, an exiled Russian journalist and analyst.

Another path is more autocracy. A different figure could replace Putin and continue his culture of repression. But Prokopenko thinks this wouldn't be another strongman dictatorship - at least not right away. These things take time, she says: at first, Putin's successor would be weaker than him, with fewer resources.

And then there's the third option: tycoons re-assert their power and Russia returns to something resembling a 1990s-style system of oligarchy. Dmitry Nekrasov, a former Kremlin adviser and opposition politician who now lives in exile, says under this scenario, the country would be governed by a handful of powerful elite clans in alliance with business interests.

This last option, of course, is the one that many tycoons want. "They'd like to return to a time when they were listened to, when they were not stripped of assets and when they understood the rules of the game," says Prokopenko, who has spent a lot of time speaking to Russia's richest people.

Though their power has been seriously curtailed since the 1990s, it's still worth listening to the tycoons: given their immense wealth, it seems likely that sooner or later they will try to re-assert their political influence.

Already, some are "trying to be friends with the right sort of security officials or ministers", says Nekrasov, the exiled politician. But he says any further steps are "too dangerous to take".

He says the behaviour of the tycoons in coming years will depend in part on their finances. Those who have lots of liquid cash will be more confident to "play political games" and jockey for position, preparing for a post-Putin country. But those whose wealth is dependent on state contracts or government goodwill will feel too afraid, in case they lose everything, he says.

Prokopenko says there's already been a shift in how the businessmen talk about Putin. They used to nickname him "Nachalnik" (which translates as "boss"), as well as "Perviy" ("first"), or by his initials "VV" - all nicknames that convey a degree of respect. Now they call him "Ded", with what Prokopenko calls "a pinch of contempt". "Ded" translates as "oldie" or "granddad" - a much less reverent name.

Some rich Russians are pining after a "return of politics into people's lives", she says, with less repression, more open speech, and healthier competition between parties and politicians.

But at the moment, she says, they are too afraid to make that happen due to Russia's stifling atmosphere. Prokopenko interviewed one tycoon who physically sat on his phone during the whole conversation, because he thought it would make digital eavesdropping more difficult for secret police. "I thought that it's an absolutely Stalinistic type of fear. It's absolutely irrational," she says.

An interesting clue for what tycoons might want from a post-Putin future came from Andrey Melnichenko, who is known as the world's fertiliser king and is currently Russia's eighth richest man.

Earlier this year, he surprised observers by giving an interview to The Economist - a rare thing for a rich Russian to do, especially to a publication from a country the Kremlin considers unfriendly. They also published an essay written by him.

In parts of the interview, Melnichenko repeated Kremlin talking points. He said that Ukraine is a battlefield between Russia and the West, and he thinks the West ignored Russia's security concerns and threatens its sovereignty.

But then it got more interesting. Melnichenko did not call for Putin to go, but - and it's a big but - he argued for a change that would bring about an end to one-man rule in Russia. He said Russia needs to engage more with the world.

Prokopenko thinks the tycoon was trying to stir a public conversation. It was a "call on rich people like him to start talking", she says.

The journalist who interviewed him, Arkady Ostrovsky, tells me the pair had "tense and heated discussions" in "hotels and cafes, mostly drinking coffee, lots of coffee, sometimes smoking". He says the tycoon seemed to be "genuinely thinking" about his answers, rather than giving politician-style spin.

Nothing in Russia is simple, and most observers think the interview probably happened with some form of approval - implicit or explicit - from the Kremlin. We don't know why authorities would have been happy to authorise the unusual call for change; it's possible they were trying to show that some degree of pluralism still exists in the country.

No tycoons came out to support him. Still, the journalist feels that Melnichenko was not speaking for himself alone, but also for his fellow businessmen.

Some of them are hoping that after Putin's departure, the country might become an "oligarchic republic", as journalist Ostrovsky puts it - something like how it looked in the 1990s, with the business elites in charge.

Based on his years of reporting on Russia, Ostrovsky says that many of the country's mega-rich currently feel a "sense of complete dead end, which this war has led Russia to… [an] absence of the future".

But even if the tycoons are thinking about the future, there's a slim prospect of them acting any time soon, it seems.

Browder, the Putin critic, says that although many of them are unhappy, they're unlikely to conspire against Putin while he is still alive. "They understand that if they were to do anything that would challenge Putin, he would kill them. And Putin is a very paranoid little man."

Mike Calvey, an American financier who used to be a key investor in Russia, agrees. "What can they do besides just go straight to the prison and lose their assets? It's easy for people who are sitting in London to say that, 'why don't you just all go stand up and go straight to prison?' That's really what would happen."

Russia's richest men used to be able to pull strings at the highest levels of power. Once Putin is gone, there is no doubt they will try to claw back their past influence. The question is: will remnants of the current regime let them?

articles.title: Blinken warns US ground invasion of Iran would be 'absolute disaster' as Tehran escalates attacks
articles.summary: Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken warned a U.S. ground invasion of Iran would be an "absolute disaster" as Tehran launched drones at Bahrain.
articles.body: Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken warned Saturday that airstrikes alone may not eliminate Iran's weapons capabilities, but said a U.S. ground invasion would be an "absolute disaster." Speaking at the 24th Hindustan Times Leadership Summit in New Delhi, Blinken, who served under President Biden, pointed to Iran's massive territory, population of roughly 90 million and ability to produce weapons deep inside the country as obstacles to any military campaign aimed at dismantling its arsenal. "The weapons that it continues to produce are back far enough, the range is great enough that you can't just take everything out," Blinken said. "You'd probably have to have a land invasion of some kind to do that, which would be an absolute disaster." TRUMP KEEPS SIGNALING AN END TO IRAN WAR, BUT EXPERT WARNS A CRUCIAL PIECE OF HIS STRATEGY IS MISSING Blinken's warning came ahead of Iran claiming Sunday to have launched six drones at a U.S. military installation in Bahrain, while reports surfaced that neighboring Iraq faced concerns that its territory could be drawn into a potential American ground operation. Bahrain said its air defenses blocked several Iranian aerial attacks Sunday, the first such interceptions since September. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted a U.S. air defense radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base with six drones in retaliation for what it described as "hostile US actions," according to Iranian state media, Reuters reported. Bahraini officials said the drones were intercepted before reaching their targets. IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS The latest escalation came amid further fighting in Yemen, where the Houthis made advances against Saudi-backed forces, raising additional concerns about the conflict spreading across the region. Blinken warned that Iran retains the ability to widen the confrontation despite the United States' overwhelming conventional military superiority. While Washington can "escalate vertically" by intensifying its bombing campaign, Blinken said, Tehran can "escalate horizontally" by targeting American military installations, regional allies and critical infrastructure, either directly or through allied armed groups. "Even though we're much more powerful, that asymmetry in their ability to escalate horizontally as opposed to vertically is not to our advantage," Blinken said. The former top diplomat also emphasized the geographic challenges facing U.S. forces. "That coastline along the Strait of Hormuz goes on forever," Blinken said. Iran is roughly four times the size of California, with a coastline and weapons production facilities that could complicate efforts to eliminate its military capabilities through air power alone. TRUMP'S MOAB THREAT COULD PUT IRAN'S DEEPEST BUNKERS IN AMERICA'S CROSSHAIRS Concerns about a potential ground operation have also intensified in neighboring Iraq, where officials have resisted proposals to sharply restrict trade and movement across the Iranian border. Iran International reported that Tehran has become concerned that Iraqi territory could be used as a staging ground for a potential U.S. operation into southern Iran. The Iraqi newspaper Al-Mada reported Nov. 9 that Iraq's prime minister privately briefed Shiite political leaders on an alleged American military plan involving a ground offensive, the outlet said. In an interview with France 24 published Friday, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein had also warned that the region's unstable security environment could not continue indefinitely. The current state of "no war and no peace" is unsustainable, Hussein said, warning that the confrontation "either goes towards peace or it goes towards war." AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR? Hussein also said Baghdad has a responsibility to pursue diplomatic mediation because Iraq has already been drawn into the conflict. He pointed to recent outreach to Tehran, including discussions with Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf. The Iraqi foreign minister also rejected a reported U.S. demand that Baghdad close all but two of its land border crossings with Iran, describing the proposed restrictions as "not possible" and "a kind of sanction against the Iraqi people." The border dispute comes as U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) expands efforts to disrupt Iranian weapons shipments and illicit trade through Task Force Iron Gate. CENTCOM announced the task force would coordinate with other U.S. agencies to prevent Iran from transporting advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illicit revenue across its land borders and the Caspian Sea. articles.title: Agniveer: Is India rethinking its short-term military recruitment scheme?
articles.summary: India has softened its recruitment scheme, giving young soldiers a longer military stint and another shot at permanent service.
articles.body:
For generations of young Indians, joining the armed forces offered something few other jobs did - a steady career, financial security, the promise of a pension after retirement and the pride of serving their country.

In 2022, the government upended that arrangement, announcing a new reform scheme under which young men and women entering the military would serve for just four years. Only a quarter would be allowed to stay on permanently. The rest would return to civilian life with a lump-sum payment, but without the pension and other benefits that had long made military service an attractive career.

Now, as the first batch of recruits prepares to complete its four-year term, the government is offering them a chance to stay longer, in a significant shift in a policy that has been fiercely debated since its introduction.

On 4 November, Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani announced that recruits who failed to secure permanent positions under the Agnipath, or "path of fire", programme would be offered another two years of service at higher pay. They would then get a second opportunity to join the regular forces, provided they met the selection criteria.

Gen Subramani said the decision followed feedback from the forces and insisted that Agnipath would continue.

But the timing is significant. More than 18,300 recruits from the first batch are due to complete their initial tenure by the end of 2026. Officials say the new arrangement will be offered to more than 300,000 Agniveers - as recruits under the scheme are known - currently serving across the army, navy and air force.

Whether future batches will also be covered remains unclear. The BBC has contacted the defence ministry for clarification.

The ministry has defended Agnipath, saying internal assessments found the recruits to be physically fit, motivated and technologically adaptable. It also said the scheme had widened recruitment across districts and made the process more standardised.

But the extension has brought renewed attention to the trade-offs at the heart of the policy - and whether its original ambitions were realistic.

When the government introduced Agnipath, it argued the scheme would reduce the average age of the armed forces, lower long-term salary and pension costs and create a younger, more technologically adaptable fighting force.

But military experts and opposition leaders have questioned whether a four-year contract could replace what had traditionally been a coveted, long-term career in the armed forces.

"Being a soldier in the armed forces was a chance for these young men to make a life for themselves, to get their families out of poor or lower-middle-income conditions," says retired Maj Gen Yash Mor, a vocal critic of the scheme.

These concerns were also amplified by the timing of Agnipath's launch. Recruitment had been suspended for nearly two years during the Covid pandemic, leaving thousands of aspirants waiting for vacancies to reopen.

The changes were greeted by massive protests across the country, with many saying the career path they had spent years preparing for had fundamentally changed.

This sentiment was felt most in states and cities that have traditionally been major recruitment hubs, where military service has been a family tradition for generations.

Kulbeer Singh Chaudhary, who runs a recruitment training institute in Dehradun city, says interest in joining the armed forces fell sharply and he stopped conducting Agniveer training batches.

The latest announcement, he hopes, would reverse that trend.

"The possibility of a longer engagement and eventual absorption into the forces may offer young candidates greater assurance," he says.

The changes also come at a time when the armed forces are facing personnel shortages. In November last year, The Indian Express reported that the army alone faced a shortfall of nearly 180,000 soldiers and was considering increasing recruitment.

But the debate over Agnipath goes beyond what happens to recruits after four years. Critics also question whether that is enough time to turn them into experienced soldiers.

Sanjiv Krishan Sood, a former additional director general of the Border Security Force, has argued that the shorter training period is particularly problematic for technical roles requiring specialised skills.

Retired Maj Gen Mor says military effectiveness depends on experience and trust built over years.

"It takes eight-to-nine years to turn a raw recruit into a dependable, seasoned soldier - someone capable of handling a tank crew, an artillery gun crew or a small detachment," he says.

"Over those years, a soldier develops the ethos, camaraderie, brotherhood and fighting spirit that bind a unit together. These qualities cannot be built overnight."

Sood says the additional two years could help improve recruits' skills, particularly in handling specialised equipment.

Senior military leaders have also welcomed the extension. Air Vice Marshal Shekhar Yadav told news agency ANI it would allow the forces to retain trained personnel for longer.

But the change could create fresh challenges within military units.

Regular soldiers, Agniveers on four-year contracts and those serving an additional two years could find themselves working alongside one another despite differences in pay, promotion prospects and post-service benefits.

Experts warn that these disparities could affect unit cohesion.

There is also the question of whether the changes will undermine one of the government's central objectives: reducing spending. Almost half of India's defence budget goes towards salaries and pensions, leaving less money for modernisation and new equipment.

By limiting the number of personnel eligible for long-term benefits, Agnipath was expected to ease that burden. But critics argue that savings should not come at the expense of military effectiveness.

"We are not against making changes, but there are ways and means to go about it," says Mor, adding that the government could instead reduce annual recruitment while retaining soldiers for longer periods.

He also points to India's tense borders with Pakistan and China, where troops remain deployed year-round, placing sustained demands on manpower and operational experience.

Retired Major-General Birender Singh Dhanoa, meanwhile, questions whether shorter service makes financial sense when the military is investing in training to operate increasingly sophisticated equipment.

"The amount of time it takes to train, and the financial outlay for training, is much higher for modern equipment. So shouldn't you get the best bang for your buck?" he asks.

Many retired officers had proposed a different approach when the scheme was announced, he says.

"We suggested that if you want to reduce your financial burden, you increase the terms and conditions of service. Take these guys for eight-or-nine years and retain a larger number after that."

The announcement also comes at a politically sensitive time. Elections are due soon in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Uttarakhand - states that have traditionally supplied large numbers of soldiers and where military recruitment remains an important source of employment.

The opposition Congress party has called the revision a "u-turn", alleging that the government is responding to fears of losing votes.

For young recruits approaching the end of their contracts, the changes offer some reassurance, but few guarantees. Two more years of service could mean more money, greater experience and another chance at a permanent career.

But for many, it also means putting their futures on hold, without knowing whether they will eventually be allowed to stay.

articles.title: ‘Suffered an anomaly’: Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites as ULA's Vulcan rocket fails minutes after launch
articles.summary: Amazon lost 40 satellites intended for its Leo internet network after a Vulcan rocket operated by United Launch Alliance (ULA) failed around 10 minutes
articles.body: Amazon lost 40 satellites intended for its Leo internet network after a Vulcan rocket operated by United Launch Alliance (ULA) failed around 10 minutes after liftoff from Florida on Sunday, marking the first mission failure for the two-decade-old launch company.The rocket, jointly owned by Boeing and Lockheed Martin, lifted off from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral at 12:40 pm local time (1740 GMT). It suffered an anomaly during flight and failed to place the satellites into orbit, ULA said in a statement."Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," the company said.ULA added that the cause of the failure was not immediately clear as it had only just occurred."Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today," it said.The failure marks a setback for ULA's flagship rocket as the company looks to establish a regular launch schedule for Amazon's expanding satellite internet constellation.Setback for Amazon's satellite internet plansAmazon has purchased 38 launches from ULA, with Vulcan expected to carry nearly half of the first generation of its Leo satellite network, which is planned to comprise 3,232 satellites, according to news agency Agence France-Presse (AFP).The failed mission was the largest batch of satellites Amazon had attempted to launch in a single flight. The company has deployed around 400 satellites since April 2025 and had not conducted any launches since July.Amazon had planned to use the constellation to launch its commercial internet service, Amazon Leo, in 2026."There is risk with any launch, and that's especially true for inaugural missions," Amazon Leo said in a post on X, adding that it believed ULA would "learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan."The failure also comes as Amazon competes with Elon Musk's Starlink in the satellite internet market.Amazon's other launch optionsAmazon is also relying on other rocket providers to deploy its satellite constellation. Jeff Bezos-founded Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, another launch vehicle expected to carry Amazon satellites, has remained grounded since an explosion during a test in May.Amazon is also a major commercial customer of French launch company Arianespace, which is scheduled to launch 36 of its satellites aboard an Ariane 6 rocket no earlier than November 23 from Kourou in French Guiana.The Vulcan failure came a day after Musk's SpaceX deployed 26 large Starlink satellites during a test flight of its Starship rocket.The flight also achieved the first-ever catch of a spacecraft using mechanical arms on its launch tower, demonstrating a step towards rocket reusability.You use AI every day. articles.title: Helen Haines: Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack
articles.summary: The MP lost both of her legs after the alleged attack outside her electorate office four weeks ago.
articles.body:
Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked with a car and left a double amputee.

The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, an incident which horrified Australia.

Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He has yet to enter pleas.

In her first public comments since the attack, Haines, 65, said she had moved into the rehabilitation stage of her recovery.

"This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Haines said.

"I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing."

She added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the generosity of well wishers who had donated to Save the Children in her honour.

Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife.

Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.

Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.

The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate.

Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had been in regular contact with Haines and her "extraordinary" family.

"All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery," he said in a statement.

"We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation."

articles.title: Yemeni forces' retreat leaves Houthis in control of key Red Sea waterway
articles.summary: Saudi-backed forces say they are moving troops from the Bab al-Mandab Strait to defend the interim capital Aden.
articles.body:
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have said they are withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaving it under the control of the Iran-backed Houthi movement.

Yemen's military said it was redeploying troops from the key shipping gateway at the southern end of the Red Sea to defend its interim capital, Aden.

The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the waterway after the Houthis seized it in a surprise offensive in September, squeezing global oil exports and prompting thousands to flee.

Houthi-run media reported later on Sunday the group had taken control of the territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.

Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis, who said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.

But the Saudi-backed forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".

The Reuters news agency reported a Southern Armed Forces statement which said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area".

It said the decision had been made with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".

The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.

The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.

Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital Sanaa.

The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: Ex-PM Johnson says 'Britain would back Brexit again' and 'zero hours ban to cost billions'
articles.summary: Some of Monday's papers lead on reaction to Burnham's bid for closer ties with the EU.
articles.body:
The former Prime Minister Boris Johnson has told the Daily Telegraph that "Britain would back Brexit again" if the country was forced into another vote on the issue - and he has urged Andy Burnham not to waste his premiership on Europe.

But writing in the Daily Mirror, the prime minister says Johnson went for a much harder Brexit than the one promised at the referendum.

Citing figures from the campaign group Stay Out, the Daily Express says a Brexit U-turn would mean Britain could have to take in around 4,400 asylum seekers every year - or pay an annual bill of £76m.

The Times says NHS and fire service leaders have warned the government that banning zero-hours contracts will put the public at risk. They say it would be impossible to employ people as emergency cover, without guaranteeing them a certain number of hours or compensating them for late shift changes. A government spokesperson tells the paper it is considering responses to its consultation and working to get the detail right.

Writing in the Guardian , the prime minister pledges to intervene early in children's lives to tackle youth unemployment, promising "a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood". Burnham promises to intervene at all the stages of life in which young people fall behind, and "long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state".

The Sun quotes Reform UK, which argues that Labour's own tax rises have made it harder for businesses to hire young people.

Writing in the Times , the Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy says she's convening senior members of the entertainment and sports industries to discuss systems to identify abusers early - and she warns them if they don't act, she'll step in. She says she believes abuse is still happening now, and cases such as Russell Brand's should be a wake-up call for us as a country.

Sir David Beckham has "kicked up a stink" because his luxury perfumes are being distributed through the budget retailer Poundland, according to the Daily Mail . The paper says his lawyers are demanding more than £30m for associating his brand with cheap, discount products. The company that produces his fragrances, Coty, has denied selling them in Poundland - but says it has the right to decide where to sell the range.

England's football victory over Spain dominates the back pages. The Daily Mirror calls it a nerve-jangling classic. The Telegraph says it was a magical night in Madrid. The Mail calls it "Spain relief." "Vamos!" is the i'Paper's headline.

articles.title: Hidden tongue movement found in Blackburn 'strong R' study
articles.summary: Dr Danielle Turton, who led the research, says generational difference in Blackburn is "fascinating".
articles.body:
Scientists have observed "hidden" tongue movements in one of the last places in England still using a distinctive pronunciation of the letter R and they also witnessed a decline in the historical sound.

By using ultrasound technology, Lancaster University researchers have been able to watch how the tongue moves during speech.

The rhoticity study focused on people in Blackburn, as its older residents still pronounce a "strong R" sound after vowels in words like star and heart.

Dr Danielle Turton, who led the research, said the findings were "fascinating" as she witnessed the centuries-old sound "gradually disappearing" as the younger generations who took part had much weaker tongue movement.

Dr Turton told BBC Radio Lancashire : "East Lancashire is one of the last places in England where people are [distinctively] pronouncing the 'R' sounds.

"But that distinctive sound we found was gradually disappearing so we went to Blackburn with an ultrasound machine - the same technology we would use to look at babies in the womb - and we used it to monitor people's tongues moving as they spoke."

She added: "What we found was so fascinating because we can see the difference between generations really clearly.

"The younger people were making weaker tongue movements. They were still doing that traditional Lancashire 'R' but they didn't have the strong tongue movements the older people were making."

She said it had been a fun study, adding it was the last sound acquired when learning to talk.

"We think of language change as something that happened hundreds of years ago but this research we can see that change happening right before our eyes in people's mouths," she said.

Dr Turton said English had changed beyond recognition over the past 1,000 years which was evident in "Shakespeare, Chaucer and particularly older texts such as Beowulf".

"However, language isn't just something that changed in the past. It is changing all around us, all the time, in such small increments that we rarely notice it happening."

"We can never observe language directly inside the brain, but we can get physically one step closer by observing the movements that create speech," she said.

"Ultrasound allows us to see tongue movements that would otherwise be completely hidden.

"What's exciting here is that we can actually monitor the physical movements involved in a sound change that's happening today."

The work forms part of a growing body of research using articulatory imaging to understand how accents change over time and how speech is produced across different communities.

The study Rhoticity in Decline? An Ultrasound Study of Lancashire /r/ was co-authored by Dr Robert Lennon and funded by the Leverhulme Trust - an independent charity providing scholarships for research and education.

articles.title: ‘Does Bengal belong to Bengalis or rogue Biharis?’ TMC MP Kalyan Banerjee's remarks on Chhath spark row
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A political row has erupted in West Bengal after Trinamool Congress (TMC) MP Kalyan Banerjee criticised the BJP government over arrangements
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A political row has erupted in West Bengal after Trinamool Congress (TMC) MP Kalyan Banerjee criticised the BJP government over arrangements for Chhath Puja, alleging that the state had been “taken over” by non-Bengalis and accusing the ruling party of undermining Bengali culture.Speaking to reporters on Saturday, Banerjee questioned the scale of decorations at Howrah railway station for the festival, alleging that similar arrangements were not made for Durga Puja.“Are there Bengalis in West Bengal anymore? Does West Bengal belong to Bengalis or rogue Biharis? Does practising Sanatan dharma mean cutting off Bengalis and establishing Biharis? BJP will destroy the Bengali culture. I was surprised to see Howrah station decked up like that for Chhath. Such decorations are not put up for Durga Puja,” he said, as quoted by news agency ANI.The TMC leader further alleged that Bengalis had become “second-category citizens” in the state and warned that they would “cease to exist” if the situation continued for another five years.His remarks drew a sharp response from West Bengal minister Indranil Khan, who accused the TMC of pursuing divisive politics and questioned its record on issues concerning Bengali culture and people.BJP minister hits back at TMCKhan alleged that neither the previous TMC government nor the Left government had adequately served the interests of Bengali people.“Is it Bengali culture to carry Maa Kali on a prison van? Is it Bengali culture to stop Durga Visarjan for Muharram? Was it in the interest of Bengalis to fire bullets on students demanding the appointment of a teacher for Bengali language at Daribhit? They do divisive politics and nothing else. Had they worked in the interest of Bengalis, 15 years of TMC rule and 34 years of Left rule would have made something good out of Bengal,” he said.Defending the arrangements for Chhath Puja, the minister said people from different communities and cultural backgrounds contributed to the country and had the right to celebrate their festivals.“Ek Bharat Shresht Bharat. People of various diversities contribute towards the country...Everyone has the right to participate in their festival, and it is the duty of the government to stand with them. But TMC and Left didn't do their duty,” Khan said.Suvendu Adhikari defends Chhath arrangementsChief minister Suvendu Adhikari also defended the government's arrangements for the festival, describing Chhath as a celebration of the Sanatan tradition and rejecting attempts to associate it exclusively with any one community or state.Adhikari participated in Chhath Puja celebrations at Ramkrishnapur Ghat in Howrah on Sunday. He said at least one crore followers of the Sanatan tradition were observing the festival and that participation was not limited to Hindi speakers.“At least one crore followers of the Sanatan tradition are observing this. It is not just Hindi speakers; all followers of the Sanatan tradition are participating in Chhath—a grand festival of faith and tradition,” he told reporters.He said the government had made arrangements for Chhath along the lines of preparations for Durga Puja, Kali Puja and Diwali, adding that the facilities for the festival were well organised.Adhikari also accused critics of indulging in “vote-bank appeasement politics” and described their approach as narrow-minded.“They would claim that the Ganpati festival belongs only to the Marathis, that Chhath belongs only to the people of Bihar, or that Ram Navami belongs only to Uttar Pradesh,” he said, adding that people had rejected such divisions and made it clear that “at the end of the day, we are all Indians”.Chhath celebrations across the countryThe political exchanges came as devotees across the country marked the final day of the four-day Chhath festival by offering 'arghya' to the rising Sun.Prime Minister Narendra Modi extended greetings to devotees on Monday, saying the festival brought together steadfast resolve and spiritual practice.In a post on X, he said, “Today, the four-day ritual of the grand festival of Chhath concluded with the offering of prayers to the rising sun. This divine festival dedicated to nature witnessed a remarkable confluence of steadfast resolve and spiritual practice. I pray to Chhathi Maiya to bestow her blessings on all the devotees observing the fast, as well as on my family members across the country.”Political leaders also participated in celebrations in several states. In Bihar, BJP national president Nitin Nabin was seen carrying a 'daura' as his wife performed the rituals in Patna, while chief minister Samrat Chaudhary offered prayers at a ghat in Munger.In Chhattisgarh, Chief minister Vishnu Deo Sai and his wife participated in the rituals in Kunkuri, where a groundbreaking ceremony for a Chhath Ghat was also held. BJP MP Ravi Kishan offered morning prayers in Gorakhpur, while party MP Manoj Tiwari participated in the celebrations at Sonia Vihar Ghat in Delhi.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
