articles.summary: NEW DELHI: BJP MP Manoj Tiwari on Monday performed the Usha Arghya rituals of Chhath Puja in Yamuna river in Delhi, accompanied by his wife, Surabhi
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP MP Manoj Tiwari on Monday performed the Usha Arghya rituals of Chhath Puja in Yamuna river in Delhi, accompanied by his wife, Surabhi Tiwari.The rituals coincided with the final day of the four-day festival, as devotees gathered along riverbanks and other water bodies across the country to offer prayers to the rising Sun.The North East Delhi MP, who hails from Purvanchal, participated in the rituals with his wife, who has been observing the festival for the third consecutive year.Speaking to news agency ANI after offering prayers, Tiwari said the banks of the Yamuna in Delhi were filled with devotees observing Chhath, with celebrations extending across a stretch of approximately 15 kilometres."The banks of the Yamuna in Delhi are filled with those observing Chhath—the celebrations extend for about 15 kilometres along this stretch. It is early morning, and the time has come to offer 'arghya' to the rising Sun God. Having already offered 'arghya' to the setting sun, we are now here at the ghat on the banks of the Yamuna in Delhi to offer it to the rising sun. There is such immense joy here--truly, a wonderful atmosphere," he said.Tiwari also said the scale of Chhath celebrations in Delhi had grown significantly, crediting the BJP-led government for making arrangements for devotees."The scale at which Chhath is being celebrated in Delhi right now is something the people here had never even imagined. At one point, Chhath celebrations on the Yamuna were even prohibited, but thanks to the government--the BJP government led by PM Modi--we have managed to put all the necessary arrangements in place," he said.Weeks earlier, the actor-turned-politician had taken a dip in the Yamuna, claiming that the river's pollution load had reduced by half over the past year due to cleaning works undertaken by the Rekha Gupta government. He had also asserted that people could once again celebrate Chhath Puja in the Yamuna, news agency PTI reported.Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi extended greetings to devotees on the conclusion of the four-day festival, saying the occasion reflected a remarkable confluence of faith, discipline and spiritual practice."Today, the four-day ritual of the grand festival of Chhath concluded with the offering of prayers to the rising sun. This divine festival dedicated to nature witnessed a remarkable confluence of steadfast resolve and spiritual practice. I pray to Chhathi Maiya to bestow her blessings on all the devotees observing the fast, as well as on my family members across the country," PM Modi posted on X.BJP chief Nitin Nabin also performed the final rituals of Chhath Puja with his wife, Deepmala, offering 'arghya' to the rising Sun.Speaking to reporters, Nabin prayed for happiness and prosperity for people across the country."I pray for the people of Bihar and the entire nation; may there be happiness and prosperity in everyone’s life," Nabin said.Nabin also described the festival as a reflection of Bihar's cultural traditions and said its message of cleanliness, purity and discipline was reaching people across the world."It is only through their blessings that we have been able to successfully conclude this four-day festival -- a period marked by rigorous discipline and physical hardship. Furthermore, the message emanating from Bihar today -- a message of cleanliness, purity, sanctity, and discipline -- is reaching the entire nation and the world. Long live Chhath Mata; long live the culture of Bihar."Former Union minister and Sambalpur MP Dharmendra Pradhan also performed Chhath Puja and offered 'arghya' to the rising Sun on Monday.Pradhan extended greetings to devotees across the country, including those in Odisha, Bihar, eastern Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand and Bengal. He said Chhath had grown into a festival of great significance and was now celebrated across the world.Speaking after offering prayers, Pradhan said devotees had the opportunity to offer 'arghya' to the setting Sun on Sunday and the rising Sun on Monday, describing it as a fortunate occasion.Chhath Puja is a four-day festival dedicated to the worship of the Sun God and Chhathi Maiya. articles.title: Martine Moise, wife of assassinated ex-Haitian leader, registers for presidential election
articles.summary: There has not been an election in Haiti since before the death of Jovenel Moise in 2021.
articles.body:
The widow of assassinated former Haitian president Jovenel Moise has registered as a presidential candidate for next year's elections in the Caribbean nation.

Martine Moise was injured in the gun attack that killed her husband at their home in the capital, Port-au-Prince, in 2021.

Haiti, which last held an election in 2016, has been plagued with chronic instability and gang violence.

Elections were scheduled to be held in December but were postponed last month until July due to the country's insecurity.

Moise has to comment on her candidacy but the electoral council website showed her registration on Sunday.

Last week she said on X: "Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently."

A total of 33 candidates have registered for the elections, including former presidents Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, former prime minister Claude Joseph and former foreign minister Dominique Dupuy.

Jovenel Moise, who led Haiti from 2017 until his death, was shot dead at his home in Port-au-Prince in July 2021 , allegedly by a group of mainly Colombian mercenaries.

Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds during the attack and was flown to a hospital in Florida.

She was charged in connection with the assassination in 2024, but the indictment was overturned last year.

The assassination shook the Caribbean nation to its core, with many Haitians shocked that the 53-year-old was killed with such apparent ease.

Thirty suspects have been indicted over the killing so far and in September 18 people were flown from Haiti to Florida to stand trial for their alleged involvement in the assassination.

Haiti has been engulfed in a wave of gang violence since the assassination of Moise.

At least 1,408 people were killed and 656 injured from April through to June this year, according to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti.

articles.title: Cycle shop owner fears break-in and rising costs will kill business
articles.summary: Gordon Kidd says if things do not improve financially, he fears his firm in Shifnal will go under.
articles.body:
The owner of a cycle shop says he is considering closing the business after a break-in and soaring costs.

Gordon Kidd, who runs Shifnal Cycles, estimates that a burglary last month cost him about £20,000 after three customer bikes and a frame were stolen and the subsequent repairs to his shop.

Along with rising bills and a "lack of government support", the former armed forces veteran said the business in Shifnal may not be viable if financial pressures continue.

A government spokesperson said that, from next year, businesses such as cycle shops would see their business rates either frozen, reduced or cut to zero, with half of the high-street retailers paying no rates.

West Mercia Police said it had received a report of a burglary on 31 October, and an investigation was ongoing.

"They stole customers' bikes, which, for me, as a shop owner, is my biggest fear," said Kidd, who was concerned the burglary could affect his reputation.

"That might put them [customers] off from using my shop, and that kills a shop."

He added: "I've got to do what's financially viable for the business.

"I've got to look at another avenue now, and I've got to look at a more cost-effective way of doing it."

Alongside coping with the impact of the burglary, Kidd called on the government to do more to help small businesses.

"I don't know how the government expects small businesses to operate and make a living," he said.

"We just break even with the repairs side of things, and it's tough."

He said the break-in "had not helped whatsoever".

"A lot of people probably think that bike shops make a lot of money when we really don't," he said.

Kidd, who not only sells cycles but also repairs and services them, told the BBC that the break-in had made him feel angry that his safe space had been invaded.

He suffers post-traumatic stress disorder and said the business was "like therapy".

"Working on bikes calms me down; it helps me keep in control of my PTSD and my mental health in general."

A government spokesperson said: "Corporation tax remains capped, and there are generous tax reliefs offered for hiring young people.

"We are also making the business environment work better through our £4.3bn business rates support package, small business plan and action on late payments.

articles.title: Film star's journey from Wolverhampton to the big screen
articles.summary: Sunjay Midda, from All Saints, says there has not been a better time in film for South Asian talent.
articles.body:
An actor from Wolverhampton has said there has never been a better time for South Asian creatives in the film industry, following the release of his new movie.

Sunjay Midda, 30, from All Saints, stars alongside Mena Massoud in Daniel and the Fiery Furnace, which premiered in the US and Canada and is now streaming on Apple TV.

Speaking to BBC Radio WM, he said his aspirations to be on the silver screen began at school when he dropped out of sixth form to pursue his career.

He said that the film industry has come a long way in showcasing representation but he thinks there is still a way to go, adding: "Our stages need to reflect society.

The actor told listeners: "Growing up in Wolverhampton, I was just a regular kid going to school. I was from an area that's known for being quite rough, it's called All Saints, but it's home to me."

With the support of his parents, he began learning about the industry and studied acting at Walsall College.

His first audition for BBC Doctors was a success and he went play the role of Shak Hanif in 93 episodes over six years.

"It was incredible being on Doctors - such a wonderful experience. I'm very just grateful for the show. It's a real shame that it's finished."

For Midda, watching the likes of Goodness Gracious Me, a British Asian comedy sketch show, East is East and Bend it Like Beckham helped pave the way for him to chase his own dreams, he said.

He added: "I'm very grateful to the likes of Kulvinder Ghir, Meera Syal and Sanjeev Bhaskar. These guys laid the foundation for us to be able to do what we do today.

"They had a dream and they pursued it. They must have come across so many stereotypical auditions and roles but what they did with Goodness Gracious Me put us on the map."

The Wulfrunian also appeared in an episode of Silent Witness, A Quiet Place: Day One and the Hulu series Death and Other Details.

Recalling some of the challenges of his career, he said: "There's been many moments I've been in that bedroom looking at my four walls thinking when's the next thing going to happen?

"It takes tenacity, perseverance and consistency. When it's not happening for me, I am so proactive. I'm going to the theatre, I'm doing acting classes, I'm writing, I'm on the phone trying to make things happen. I feel like you have to be in this industry.

"Especially as a South Asian, you've got to kick the doors down sometimes."

For his latest project, which was filmed in Rajasthan, India, the drama gave him the chance to channel his Christian roots and further explore his faith, he said.

"It's based on a biblical story of these three young lads who had to put their faith to the test.

"I was playing one of the young lads, Shadrack, and it was just a wonderful experience, delving into the scriptures, understanding what it was like in those days, and also finding it relatable to today's life.

"I grew up Christian and I had a whole faith journey myself and, when I got the call to play the role, it felt like it was meant to be."

Looking forward, he said: "We need to see more authentic casting. I think it's happening, I'm grateful my background is Indian. I just did a Middle-Eastern role, so I'm definitely being cast more authentically towards diverse characters."

articles.title: Alan Milburn’s Neets review: Why some young people don’t go to school
articles.summary: As a landmark report is published, the BBC speaks to school avoiders and those trying to fix the issue.
articles.body:
Thirteen-year-old Eva hadn't been to school for 15 months before September.

She describes how she used to get up every morning, try to get ready for school and get stuck by the front door.

"It's like a physical barrier that you can't cross and you can't move," she recalls.

"If I was able to get in the car, we'd drive to school," she continues. "I'd probably normally either faint or throw up while we were sat in the car park."

Eva's one of the thousands of school pupils in England who misses more than half the academic year. Experts say that children who miss school are more at risk of becoming Neet - not in employment, education or training. A government-commissioned review into how to solve the problem of nearly one million young people being Neet is due to be published on Tuesday.

Eva is autistic and stopped going to school after struggling with the transition to secondary education.

Every morning, one of Eva's parents would call her teachers to tell them she wouldn't be going in that day, and she says she would stay at home watching YouTube videos and episodes of Horrible Histories "just to try and keep up".

This year, she has started at an alternative provision school which has smaller class sizes, therapy animals and more freedom to take breaks. But she still worries about her future and whether her record of school avoidance might turn off future employers.

Eva recognises that many older people will assume "tough love" is the answer, and that they might even call pupils like her lazy - but she believes the situation is more complex.

"We're not lazy, we want to go, we want to do something, we want to live our lives, but we can't," she says.

Total school absence numbers have fallen since their peak during the pandemic but they're yet to return to pre-Covid levels.

In the autumn and spring terms of the 2025/26 academic year, the overall absence rate was 6.6%, down from 7.38% in 2021/2022 but much higher than pre-pandemic levels, which were below 5%.

The latest figures published in October show that 168,000 pupils (2.32%) were classed as severely absent - missing more than half of their classes - in the 2025/2026 autumn and spring terms. Back in spring 2019, this figure was under 60,000.

Experts are concerned that this absence will translate into worse outcomes for thousands of young people.

New analysis from the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ) shows that 133,000 of today's persistently absent GCSE pupils (those missing more than 10% of school) are on course to spend a year or more being Neet. Similar research from the National Centre for Social Research linked persistent absence to much higher rates of not being in work, education or training between the ages of 16 and 24.

"Ministers must recognise that getting children back into school is the first step to getting young people into work," says Dan Lilley, head of youth at the Centre for Social Justice.

"That means restoring the expectation that children are in school every day."

Research suggests many parents may be comfortable with regular school absences. CSJ polling found that 44% of parents think it reasonable for a child to miss one in every 10 school days – the threshold for persistent absence.

In response to the CSJ research, the Department for Education said it was "helping tackle the barriers that stop children attending school, through free breakfast clubs in every primary school, better mental health support and earlier help for pupils with special educational needs".

Autism and ADHD can contribute to children avoiding school, says Sheila Griffiths, who co-founded the charity Hope4More in Crewe after her own son struggled to attend school.

"The classroom environment doesn't suit [those children], so we support them here," she explains.

Hope4More runs art classes that combine creativity and business skills, and it also supports parents to ask for the help they need from schools or their local authority to get their child back into education.

"We've got families here who have already had to give up work. They're struggling. It's so stressful the situations they end up in."

Sheila also runs a programme at Cheshire College South & West to help young people with the transition into further education.

She says: "With our older ones, so perhaps the ones that should be in year 10 or 11, we work with them at college and then they get used to being in that environment which is different to school, but it's also still quite busy."

Paul Browne, who is one of the assistant principals there, says: "Especially since Covid, there's a lot of learners who are not engaging in education. The thought of coming into a mainstream college is quite a big step for them.

"We're seeing [most of] our students now are more like they were before Covid, where doing exams and coming to college is the norm. But there's still that small cohort [who struggle] and it's about getting them ready and helping them back into education."

Mali, 18, stopped attending school three years ago in year 10.

"We didn't do our Sats because that's when the first lockdown hit," she recalls.

"It was so isolating and so strange, but I loved it. I was able to sit in my own room and do schoolwork.

"Going back into school, it was difficult. I started struggling with panic attacks a lot, to the point where I was being pulled out of classes."

Mali was diagnosed with autism when she was 15. After she stopped attending school, her mental health deteriorated to the point where she didn't leave her bedroom.

"It was like the second I got past my doorframe, my whole body would stop. My legs would go numb, my head would tense. It felt like I was dying. I can't explain it any other way."

"I do get quite emotional about it. I feel like I've tried so hard and I went to school for so long and I went through so much and I have nothing to show for it. I don't have my GCSEs, I didn't even do my Sats."

articles.title: Thrift shop donors asked to choose which charities receive funds
articles.summary: The owners want customers and donors to decide what charities benefit each month.
articles.body:
Shoppers and donors at a new charity shop will be able to help decide which organisations benefit from the money it raises.

Twisted Sisters Thrift Store, in Tunstall opened last week, and is inviting customers to nominate causes they would like to support, with a different charity set to receive donations each month.

Owner Julie Rindam said the idea came after the closure of a charity shop; she had run for eight years.

"The pastor is retiring and it was either another empty shop or I took it on."

Rindam said many of the shop's regular donors wanted to continue supporting charitable causes, leading to the idea of allowing the community to decide where the money goes.

"All my donators still wanted to drop off to us, so we thought, well, how about a different charity every month?" she said.

"We ask all the donators who they'd like us to donate to, so every month it will be a different charity benefiting."

Rather than supporting a single organisation, the shop plans to keep a record of suggestions, being completely transparent with customers and donors before selecting a charity at the end of each month.

"Everyone who drops off, we ask and we keep a book and every month we'll pick a different charity to benefit from, whether that's City Dogs Home, Cancer Research, Diabetes or other charities," Rindam said.

Shop manager Jeanette Worthington said the approach was designed to ensure local people remained involved in how the money was distributed.

As well as raising money for charity, the store also aims to act as a community hub, offering free food, sanitary products, contraception and school uniforms when available.

Worthington said supporting local people was just as important as supporting charities.

"People know they can come here, it's a safe space," she said.

"We will help anybody if we have the time and if we can't do it, we'll say come back at such and such a time."

Regular customer and donor Janet Smart said the shop had become a valuable part of the community.

"When I'm decluttering everything, it comes to here because I know they don't charge a lot. People haven't got much money today," she said.

"You meet such nice people in here as well."

She added that the social side of the shop was equally important.

"I think for people on their own, it's nice to be able to come in somewhere and people chat with them."

Shopper Jack Spencer said the store offered affordable options for people who might otherwise struggle to buy certain items.

"It feels a lot more personal, a lot more out there. You go in, you don't know what you're going to walk into, it changes constantly," he said.

"You might find something that you could have been looking for, but you just couldn't afford it."

For Rindam and Worthington, the hope is that both the charities and the local community will benefit.

articles.title: Bristol father and son shortlisted for Waterstones book award
articles.summary: Dan Ojari and his eight-year-old son Finn sparked the idea during a routine arts and crafts evening.
articles.body:
A father and son have been shortlisted for Waterstones Book of the Year after turning an arts and crafts evening at home into a children's picture book.

Dan Ojari and his eight-year-old son Finn, from Bristol, coined the idea for Is This a Plum? after noticing potential in the shapes left behind after cutting out paper.

Dan said he hoped it would inspire creativity in the next generation, adding: "Now, more than ever, we need children to spread their unique silliness and simple wisdom."

The playful rhyming book featuring interactive cut-outs is among 20 recommended books on the shortlist. The winner will be announced on 26 November.

Dan said the idea came while he was cutting out his son's drawings one evening, when the pair noticed how the negative space created new shapes on the paper underneath.

"So we instantly thought, how can we make this based around a bum?" he laughed.

"That's the joy of working and making things with kids. There's a sort of honesty and simplicity they bring to whatever you're doing - and a lot of comedy."

Every year, Waterstones booksellers are called on to nominate an outstanding book of any genre that they most enjoyed recommending to readers this year.

Dan said making the shortlist had been an "unexpected" surprise.

"We hope it inspires other kids to get drawing, writing and making things to share with the world," he said.

The father-of-two also works as an animation director at Aardman studios, surrounded by "amazing craftspeople" who "love what they do and want to get it right".

He said; "The job that I have is constantly trying to think of funny and creative things but I think everyone has that in them."

Dan said many of their designs were created when Finn was just four years old.

"We absolutely made it together and I think that is why it's so fun and different - because Finn helped make it," he said.

"It's very easy to read and will probably make you laugh at least once," Finn added.

articles.title: Experts explore returning beavers to River Waveney in Suffolk
articles.summary: A trust says the river-dwelling mammals could improve the health of the waterway.
articles.body:
A river separating two counties could become home to beavers as work begins to explore where a colony could be introduced.

The River Waveney Trust is in conversation with Natural England and other agencies about potentially reintroducing the river-dwelling mammals along the River Waveney.

The 59-mile (95km) waterway rises in Redgrave and Lopham Fen in Suffolk and heads east, creating a border between Norfolk and Suffolk as it flows out into the River Yare at Great Yarmouth.

Ange Lamb, catchment resilience officer, said the upper reaches of the River Waveney and its tributaries could make ideal environments for beavers. If successful, beavers could return by 2029.

Known as river engineers, beavers were native to Britain but they were hunted to extinction by the end of the 16th century.

Conservationists want to reintroduce them to help boost the health of waterways through their ability to create wetland areas.

But there are concerns, particularly around dams being built in inappropriate places and their ability to destroy trees.

Beavers have been reintroduced already in Norfolk at enclosures at Sculthorpe Moor Nature Reserve near Fakenham, Wild Ken Hill near King's Lynn and on the iver Glaven near Holt.

A pair of beavers have also been spotted in the wild at Pensthorpe Natural Park, which is a short distance downstream from Sculthorpe Moor.

In Suffolk, a colony was introduced at Little Haugh Hall at Norton, near Bury St Edmunds.

River Waveney Trust is holding a series of events to discuss the proposals and it hopes to engage with local landowners in Bungay, Palgrave and Eye.

Lamb added: "Our aim is to ensure that local communities, landowners, anglers and conservation groups have the opportunity to be part of the discussion from the beginning."

While talks are beginning, Lamb said it would be years before any decision would be made, which would require a licence from Natural England.

More information about the events can be found on its website.
